The programme combines engineering, geoscience, real-time monitoring, regulatory research and Indigenous, community and public engagement. The award supports research and a proposed demonstration trajectory; it is not an offshore injection permit, does not confirm that injection has begun and does not establish verified removal credits.
source: Canada New Frontiers in Research Fund / Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council
status_note: Six-year NFRF-supported project announced in 2025 with research, monitoring and demonstration objectives.

document_title: Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement Model Intercomparison Project (OAEMIP)
notes: Carbon to Sea and Google are supporting a three-year international model intercomparison project that applies common experimental protocols to compare estimates of ocean alkalinity enhancement efficiency across locations, seasons, future climate conditions and model structures. OAEMIP is intended to improve comparability, identify model uncertainty and establish rigorous modeling standards for responsible OAE research. It is a coordinated research programme rather than a field deployment, environmental permit, carbon-credit protocol or confirmation of achieved atmospheric carbon removal.
source: Carbon to Sea Initiative / Google
status_note: Launched in March 2025; a January 2026 update confirmed the coordinating research fellows and active international modeling work.

document_title: CARSAFE — Carbon Sinks on Subarctic Shelves, Fjords and Estuaries
notes: CARSAFE is one of four transnational projects recommended for funding under the 2026 JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems. The project will use sediment cores and complementary observations from Scandinavia and eastern Canada to reconstruct carbon burial, pelagic fluxes, oxidation and hypoxia, and will develop an open Subarctic Blue Carbon Dashboard. The recommendation is pending completion of contractual arrangements; the project has not yet reported results, verified additional carbon removal or created a deployment or crediting mechanism.
source: JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems
status_note: Recommended for funding on 9 July 2026; contractual details remained to be completed and the project was expected to begin by December 2026.

document_title: C-SCALE — Constraining Carbon Stocks and Greenhouse-Gas Fluxes Across High-Latitude Marsh Ecosystems
notes: C-SCALE is one of four projects recommended for funding under the JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems. It will quantify carbon sequestration, methane and nitrous-oxide fluxes, inorganic carbon and alkalinity across high-latitude salt marshes and assess how warming and sea-level rise affect net climate benefits. The project is intended to improve indicators and comparable evidence, but the funding recommendation was still subject to contracts and does not represent a restoration authorization, quantified removal claim or carbon-credit methodology.
source: JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems
status_note: Recommended for funding on 9 July 2026; contractual details remained to be completed and the project was expected to begin by December 2026.

country_or_region: Ireland, Germany, Poland, Norway and Greece
document_title: BluePaths — Enhancing the Science, Policy and Impact Pathway for Blue Carbon in Europe
notes: BluePaths is one of four projects recommended for funding under the JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems. It will address data gaps, lateral carbon fluxes, restoration effectiveness, site selection and human pressures while strengthening links between blue-carbon science, management and policy across several European countries. The recommendation does not itself implement restoration, adopt a European accounting standard, issue credits or verify additional carbon removal, and funding contracts were still pending.
source: JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems
status_note: Recommended for funding on 9 July 2026; contractual details remained to be completed and the project was expected to begin by December 2026.

document_title: MAGIEC — Mudflats Across Gradients of Human Impact and Environmental Extreme: Blue Carbon Cycling
notes: MAGIEC is one of four projects recommended for funding under the JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems. The project will examine carbon sequestration and retention in unvegetated mudflats across transatlantic sites, including effects of nutrient pollution, chemical contamination, extreme events, sediment mineralogy, microbial communities and invasive species, and will support standardized protocols and management guidance. Contracts were not yet complete, and the recommendation does not establish a restoration project, carbon-credit method or verified removal outcome.
source: JPI Oceans Joint Call on Blue Carbon Ecosystems
status_note: Recommended for funding on 9 July 2026; contractual details remained to be completed and the project was expected to begin by December 2026.

subnational_area: Locally designed coastal and marine projects in developing countries
document_title: Blue Natural Capital Financing Facility — Phase 3
notes: The Government of Luxembourg and IUCN launched the third phase of the Blue Natural Capital Financing Facility to provide tailored technical assistance and finance preparation for locally designed coastal and marine projects. The facility has a history of supporting mangrove, seagrass, coral-reef and protected-area initiatives and applies environmental, social and community safeguards when developing investable projects. Phase 3 is broader than carbon removal, does not guarantee that every supported project will quantify additional sequestration, and does not itself issue carbon credits, certify removals or authorize ecosystem interventions.
source: Government of Luxembourg / International Union for Conservation of Nature

document_title: Public Law 119-74 — Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026
notes: The enacted fiscal year 2026 appropriations package, together with its incorporated explanatory statement, provides federal funding direction for NOAA, the National Oceanographic Partnership Program and related science agencies to continue research, external grants and public-private work relevant to marine carbon dioxide removal, including safe evaluation, measurement and responsible research development. The law funds research directions rather than authorizing a particular ocean intervention, approving a field site, establishing a federal carbon-credit methodology or certifying achieved removals.
source: United States Congress / U.S. Government Publishing Office
status_note: Approved and enacted as Public Law 119-74 on 23 January 2026 for fiscal year 2026 appropriations.

document_title: Carbon Dioxide Removal Leadership Act of 2026 (H.R. 9975)
notes: The House bill would require the U.S. Department of Energy to procure net carbon dioxide removal from ambient air or seawater against rising annual targets and would require lifecycle accounting, independent third-party verification and federal standards for measurement, monitoring, reporting and verification. The ONCE-relevant component is direct removal from seawater; the bill also covers non-marine direct-air approaches. It was introduced but not enacted, so the procurement obligations, tonnage targets and MRV rules are proposals rather than active requirements.
source: United States Congress / U.S. Government Publishing Office
status_note: Introduced in the House of Representatives on 27 July 2026 and referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce; not enacted.

document_title: Carbon Dioxide Removal Leadership Act of 2026 (S. 5170)
notes: The Senate bill would require the U.S. Department of Energy to procure net carbon dioxide removal from ambient air or seawater against rising annual targets and would require lifecycle accounting, independent third-party verification and federal standards for measurement, monitoring, reporting and verification. The ONCE-relevant component is direct removal from seawater; the bill also covers non-marine direct-air approaches. It was introduced but not enacted, so the procurement obligations, tonnage targets and MRV rules are proposals rather than active requirements.
source: United States Congress / U.S. Government Publishing Office
status_note: Introduced in the Senate on 29 July 2026 and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; not enacted.

document_title: NESP Project 1.5 — Scoping for an Australian Wetland Inventory: Identifying Knowledge Gaps and Solutions for Mapping Australian Marine and Coastal Wetlands
notes: This completed National Environmental Science Program project assessed the information and institutional gaps affecting a future Australian marine and coastal wetland inventory. Blue-carbon mapping was one of five explicit work areas. The project recommended integrated maps of blue-carbon habitats below the highest astronomical tide, historical and pre-clearance habitat maps, field verification of carbon-stock maps, strategic sampling across geomorphic settings, mapping of restoration co-benefits, and modelling of climate-driven changes in blue-carbon stocks and sequestration. The outputs were designed to support a national wetland inventory and ecosystem-accounting applications. The project was a scoping and evidence-building exercise: it did not establish a carbon-crediting method, issue credits, approve restoration projects, or quantify additional carbon removal from an implemented intervention.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Completed NESP Marine and Coastal Hub project; the published project page reports final findings and recommendations.

subnational_area: Fitzroy Basin, Peel-Harvey and South West catchments, and Ord River floodplain
document_title: NESP Project 1.15 — Coastal Wetland Restoration for Carbon Accounting
notes: This completed National Environmental Science Program project examined whether historically modified coastal wetlands could be restored and financed through blue-carbon markets. It developed a site-selection process, estimated carbon-abatement potential, assessed regulatory and policy constraints, compared carbon-price scenarios, and evaluated ecological, cultural and economic co-benefits. The project identified potentially eligible restoration areas in the Fitzroy Basin and Peel-Harvey case-study regions and reported modelled annual abatement estimates for those areas. It also found that the assessed Ord River sites did not satisfy the relevant restoration eligibility conditions. The work provides feasibility, accounting and investment evidence, but it did not itself rewet the identified sites, issue carbon credits, create an approved national methodology, or grant a deployment authorization.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Completed NESP Marine and Coastal Hub project with published findings, datasets and restoration-site assessment outputs.

document_title: NESP Project 3.5 — Partnerships for Seagrass Research and Protection
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project consolidates historical seagrass information, fills priority survey gaps, develops new spatial datasets, evaluates monitoring technologies, and makes information available to regional planners, Traditional Owners and Indigenous rangers. A formally approved 2026 variation adds national-scale data collation and a seagrass-fragmentation index derived from drone and satellite imagery. The project page states that these outputs will support Blue Carbon assessments, national environmental accounting and State of the Environment reporting. Its principal contribution is the habitat-data and monitoring foundation needed for future blue-carbon assessment; it does not quantify verified carbon removals, establish a carbon-credit methodology, authorize restoration, or create a market registry.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP project; an approved variation began in 2026 to extend data collation and develop a nationally relevant seagrass-fragmentation index.

subnational_area: Tasmania — Tayaritja / Furneaux Group of Islands
document_title: NESP Project 3.6 — Exploring the Distribution and Ecological Value of Seagrass at the Furneaux Islands, Tasmania
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project mapped the extent, composition, population structure and blue-carbon value of temperate seagrass beds in Tayaritja Sea Country in partnership with the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre. It combined historical data, satellite remote sensing, field validation, video surveys and rhizome coring, and produced public datasets on seagrass extent, habitat composition and blue-carbon stocks. The project also developed consistent, standards-based approaches for collecting, analysing, managing and reporting environmental data and strengthened Indigenous-led monitoring capacity. The work identifies potential areas for future blue-carbon projects, but it did not issue credits, approve a restoration intervention, establish additionality or permanence rules, or report verified project-level carbon removal.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Project period reported as 2023–2025; datasets and project outputs are publicly available.

document_title: NESP Project 3.8 — Feral-Ungulate Control to Reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Wetlands
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project tests whether controlling feral pigs, cattle and buffalo can provide a scientifically defensible wetland greenhouse-gas abatement activity. It quantifies emissions under different disturbance and control scenarios, evaluates costs and potential returns, develops baselines, validates monitoring and verification techniques, and explores remotely sensed tools for national-scale reporting. The work is intended to support a possible carbon-abatement methodology and future access to Australian carbon and nature-repair markets. A 2026 project variation strengthens national-scale assessment tools. The project remains an evidence and method-development activity: the cited draft methodology is not evidence that a government-approved crediting method, registered offset project, issued credit or deployment authorization already exists.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP project with an approved 2026 variation focused on national-scale monitoring and reporting tools.

subnational_area: Northern Australian Indigenous land and sea country
document_title: NESP Project 3.20 — Supporting Indigenous People’s Participation in Environmental Markets
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project develops the knowledge, networks and decision processes required for Indigenous organisations to participate in Australian blue-carbon and coastal environmental-repair markets. It identifies legal, tenure, resource-ownership and co-benefit barriers; co-designs participation guides and regional information products; maps relevant opportunities; and develops protocols concerning free, prior and informed consent. Its expected outputs include a decision framework and clearer pathways for Indigenous-led management and market participation. The project addresses market readiness, governance and safeguards rather than creating a carbon market itself. It does not issue credits, certify projects, determine ownership in individual cases, approve a blue-carbon activity, or demonstrate quantified carbon removal.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP research and co-design project; the source page does not state a formal closure date.

document_title: NESP Project 4.10 — De-risking Nature Repair Activities in Australian Coastal and Marine Ecosystems
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project compiles a national evidence base on coastal and marine nature-repair activities, updates restoration databases, examines project risks and outcomes, and drafts a national framework to guide coordinated investment. The project explicitly addresses participation in blue-carbon markets and the need to reduce uncertainty for governments, communities, Indigenous groups, non-profit organisations and private investors. It is intended to improve project evaluation, investment decisions and governance rather than to operate a crediting system. The programme covers a broad range of marine and coastal restoration activities, so it is included for its explicit blue-carbon market and investment component; it does not itself issue carbon credits, approve individual restoration projects, establish a binding national framework, or quantify verified removals.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP project developing evidence, databases and a draft national framework for coastal and marine nature repair.

document_title: NESP Project 4.12 — Gulf of Carpentaria Mangrove Dieback: Research to Support Recovery Management
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project evaluates the condition and recovery of shoreline mangroves damaged by major dieback events in the Gulf of Carpentaria. It updates condition maps, conducts aerial and field monitoring, quantifies carbon in damaged, undamaged and recovering stands, evaluates protection and restoration options, and includes mitigation works or small-scale trials where feasible. The project is designed to support a costed management response plan and future rehabilitation decisions. Its carbon component measures changes in mangrove carbon stocks and supports restoration planning, but the project does not establish a carbon-credit methodology, authorize commercial deployment, set a quantified removal target, or report issued credits or independently verified additional removals.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP project; monitoring and recovery research continued through at least 2026.

document_title: ARC Discovery Project DP200100575 — Formation and Stabilisation of Coastal Blue Carbon
notes: This Australian Research Council Discovery Project investigated the composition, formation, stability and vulnerability of organic carbon stored in seagrass meadows, mangrove forests and tidal marshes. It combined analytical chemistry and environmental microbiology to determine how coastal blue carbon is stabilised or destabilised and to improve modelling of carbon-cycle feedbacks. The grant was intended to inform management of coastal vegetated ecosystems for climate mitigation and carbon-offset potential. The funded research period ended in December 2025. The project generated scientific evidence rather than a regulatory instrument: it did not create an approved offset method, issue credits, authorize restoration, or demonstrate a quantified additional removal project.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Grant period ended on 30 December 2025; the ARC portal may continue to display an administrative status of Active.

document_title: ARC Discovery Project DP210100739 — Mangrove Sustainability on the Australian Coast
notes: This Australian Research Council Discovery Project models how Australian mangrove shorelines and adjoining communities respond to sea-level rise. It produces maps and spatial models of mangrove change, evaluates implications for blue-carbon stocks, quantifies future sequestration and stored carbon, and supports national carbon-accounting and coastal-planning efforts. The current ARC grant record reports an anticipated end date of 31 December 2026. The project provides research, modelling and accounting evidence; it does not itself protect or restore a specified area, establish a national accounting rule, issue carbon credits, or provide a deployment authorization.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Active ARC Discovery Project; current grant data report an anticipated end date of 31 December 2026.

document_title: ARC Discovery Project DP200100546 — Effect of Elevated Nutrients on Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles in Seagrass Beds
notes: This Australian Research Council Discovery Project investigates how human-driven nutrient enrichment changes carbon and nitrogen cycling in seagrass beds. It uses whole-ecosystem stable-isotope labelling and field measurements to examine the amount and form of carbon and nitrogen exported to the ocean or buried in sediments. The project is intended to improve global carbon-budget knowledge and coastal-management predictions. The current ARC record reports an anticipated end date in December 2026. This is fundamental research and does not constitute a seagrass restoration programme, a carbon-crediting method, a monitoring standard for offset projects, or authorization for a carbon-removal intervention.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Active ARC Discovery Project; current grant data report an anticipated end date of 15 December 2026.

document_title: ARC DECRA DE240100115 — Evaluating the Impact and Efficiency of Engineering the Ocean to Remove Carbon Dioxide from the Atmosphere
notes: This Australian Research Council DECRA project evaluates a suite of marine carbon-dioxide-removal strategies using new observations of zooplankton grazing, an improved marine biogeochemical model, and coupled ocean, atmosphere and fisheries models. It estimates long-term sequestration efficiency and potential effects on fisheries catch to inform scientific, policy and industry decisions about whether and how ocean geoengineering should proceed. The funded period runs through the end of 2026. The project is model-based research: it does not authorize or conduct a commercial marine-geoengineering deployment, create an MRV standard, approve a carbon-credit methodology, or demonstrate verified removals in the ocean.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Active ARC DECRA project, 1 January 2024–31 December 2026.

subnational_area: Australian coastal ecosystems and continental shelf
document_title: ARC DECRA DE250100125 — Emerging Blue Carbon Pathways as Natural Climate Solutions
notes: This Australian Research Council DECRA project quantifies two under-accounted coastal carbon pathways: export of carbon from vegetated coastal ecosystems to the deep sea and storage of carbon in unvegetated continental-shelf sediments. It combines experiments, oceanographic modelling, offshore sediment mapping and disturbance-vulnerability assessment. Expected outputs include high-resolution carbon-stock information for Australia’s National Ocean Account, cost-effective accounting models and a tool to verify the climate benefits of managing coastal ecosystems. The project is active through early 2028. Its models and verification tool are research outputs and are not yet an approved carbon-credit methodology, a government MRV standard, a registered project or evidence of issued credits.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Active ARC DECRA project, 3 October 2025–2 January 2028.

document_title: ARC Linkage Project LP250200320 — Advancing Seagrass Restoration to Ecologically Relevant Scales in Australia
notes: This Australian Research Council Linkage Project develops the evidence and practical framework needed to expand seagrass restoration to ecologically relevant scales. It evaluates propagule supply, best-practice site selection, recovery of ecosystem services and the design of large-scale restoration trials. The official grant record explicitly identifies carbon storage and capture as benefits of restored seagrass and links the work to national climate and biodiversity targets. The project runs from 2026 to 2029 and includes university, government, foundation and Traditional Owner partners. It is a research and demonstration programme, not a binding restoration mandate, carbon-credit method, project permit, quantified national removal target or evidence of verified credits.
source: Australian Research Council
status_note: Active ARC Linkage Project, 1 January 2026–31 December 2029.

document_title: NERC Studentship 2607215 — Establishing Marine Biodiversity Baselines for Blue Carbon Habitats
notes: This UK Natural Environment Research Council studentship established biodiversity baselines and monitoring tools for priority blue-carbon habitats, including maerl beds, seagrass beds, intertidal mudflats and coastal saltmarsh. The work synthesised the role of marine invertebrates in carbon sequestration and storage, built a DNA-barcode reference library and tested environmental-DNA methods for future habitat monitoring. The project ran from September 2021 to March 2025 and is listed as closed. It improved ecological monitoring capacity but did not quantify additional carbon removal from a management intervention, create a carbon accounting or crediting methodology, authorize restoration, or issue credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council
status_note: Closed NERC studentship, September 2021–March 2025.

subnational_area: Orkney Islands and Scapa Flow, Scotland
document_title: NERC Studentship 2337736 — Underpinning Marine Spatial Planning of Blue Carbon Resources: Orkney Islands Catchment Audit Case Study
notes: This UK Natural Environment Research Council studentship developed a regional blue-carbon audit for Orkney and Scapa Flow to support marine spatial planning. It combined ecosystem modelling, mapping and fieldwork to address data gaps concerning carbon stocks and fluxes in kelp forests, maerl beds, horse-mussel beds, flame-shell beds, seagrass meadows, brittlestar beds and bryozoan thickets. The project worked alongside the Orkney Islands Council Marine Planning Team and ran from September 2019 to March 2023. It produced planning and accounting evidence, but it did not establish a statutory marine plan, approve a crediting method, certify blue-carbon assets, issue credits or authorize a carbon-removal intervention.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council
status_note: Closed NERC studentship, September 2019–March 2023.

document_title: MAR-CO2 — Measurement and Reporting for Responsible Marine CO2 Removal
notes: MAR-CO2 is a Horizon Europe project developing fit-for-purpose monitoring, reporting and verification systems for marine carbon-dioxide removal. It will co-design, refine and test tools for quantifying removal additionality and durability, assessing ecological risks and co-benefits, and developing governance arrangements that support transparency, fairness and public trust. The project combines observations, experiments, modelling, ecology, social science, governance and digital-twin methods, and tests the tools under operational mCDR conditions with industry partners. The grant was signed in May 2026 and the project runs from August 2026 to July 2030. It is an international research and standard-development programme; it does not itself issue carbon credits, create binding EU permitting rules, approve commercial deployments or guarantee that tested removals will qualify under a compliance market.
source: European Commission — Horizon Europe / CORDIS
status_note: Horizon Europe project active from 1 August 2026 to 31 July 2030; grant agreement signed on 6 May 2026.

document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market Phase 1: Nitrogen and Coastal Blue Carbon
notes: This NOAA-supported collaborative research project examined how salt-marsh carbon storage and greenhouse-gas fluxes respond to nitrogen pollution, tidal conditions and wetland management. It developed monitoring, modeling and practitioner-facing tools intended to make coastal blue-carbon information usable in conservation and restoration decisions. Outputs included a coastal-wetland greenhouse-gas model, guidance on applying the Verified Carbon Standard methodology for tidal-wetland and seagrass restoration, economic and policy communication materials, and stakeholder training. The project helped establish the scientific and procedural foundation for considering wetland carbon finance. It was a completed research and capacity-building project; it did not itself authorize restoration work, create a compliance market, register a carbon project or issue carbon credits.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from November 2011 to June 2015.

document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market Phase 2: Expanding Blue Carbon Implementation
notes: The second phase expanded the earlier Massachusetts blue-carbon work into a broader implementation-oriented research programme for New England and the Mid-Atlantic coast. The project verified and generalized a model for estimating wetland greenhouse-gas fluxes and potential carbon storage from a limited set of accessible environmental variables. It also completed a carbon-market feasibility assessment for the proposed Herring River wetland restoration project and produced tools, education products and guidance for managers and decision-makers. The programme reduced information and transaction barriers associated with blue-carbon project preparation, but it remained a scientific assessment and capacity-building activity. It did not approve the Herring River project, establish a mandatory accounting rule, register offsets or demonstrate that any credits had been issued.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from January 2016 to September 2019.

document_title: Pacific Northwest Carbon Stocks and Blue Carbon Database Project
notes: This regional collaborative project conducted the first comprehensive assessment of carbon stocks across major Pacific Northwest tidal-wetland classes and created a user-oriented regional blue-carbon database. Field and compiled data covered seagrass, low marsh, high marsh and forested tidal wetlands across distinct coastal settings. The work was designed to support greenhouse-gas accounting, restoration planning, conservation prioritization and assessment of possible carbon-finance opportunities. It strengthened the evidence base needed by managers and project developers rather than establishing a market mechanism itself. The completed project did not authorize a restoration intervention, certify a methodology, register a carbon-credit project or guarantee that mapped carbon stocks represented additional and creditable removals. Subsequent project-level feasibility and policy decisions remained separate steps.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from November 2016 to December 2019.

document_title: Feasibility Planning for Pacific Northwest Blue Carbon Finance Projects
notes: This catalyst project assessed whether carbon finance could contribute to tidal-wetland conservation and restoration in the Pacific Northwest. The project evaluated baseline and restoration scenarios and examined financial feasibility for candidate sites in the Snohomish, Skagit and Coos estuaries. It drew on regional carbon-stock data and the Verified Carbon Standard tidal-wetland and seagrass methodology to identify opportunities, data gaps, transaction constraints and next steps for project development. The work supplied project proponents, resource managers and potential investors with a structured feasibility assessment. It did not constitute validation or registration under a carbon standard, did not authorize work at any candidate site and did not demonstrate that credits were issued. Project-level additionality, ownership, permanence, leakage and monitoring requirements would still require formal assessment.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed catalyst project, implemented from September 2018 to December 2019.

subnational_area: Alaska — Lower Kenai Peninsula and Kachemak Bay
document_title: Assessing Kachemak Bay's Blue Carbon Resources
notes: The project developed local capacity to assess and communicate blue-carbon resources in the Lower Kenai region of Alaska. It built on pilot salt-marsh measurements and combined wetland and peatland carbon assessment approaches with stakeholder engagement, conservation planning and information on possible carbon-market applications. Technical partners supported field protocols and helped place regional carbon stores within a broader conservation-finance context. The project was intended to improve the evidence available to municipalities, agencies and nonprofit organizations considering protection of vulnerable wetlands. It did not establish a carbon-credit programme, issue offsets, transfer ownership of stored carbon or authorize land-use restrictions. Carbon valuation and financing opportunities identified through the work remained exploratory and would require site-specific legal, ecological, additionality and monitoring review.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed science-transfer project, implemented from November 2017 to June 2019.

subnational_area: Texas and the Gulf of Mexico coast
document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market on the Gulf Coast
notes: This NOAA-funded science-transfer project adapted lessons from the Massachusetts Bringing Wetlands to Market initiative for Gulf Coast audiences. It used outreach dialogues, stakeholder needs assessment and communication products to explain coastal blue carbon, natural capital and the potential role of carbon finance in supporting wetland restoration and conservation. The work connected landowners, resource managers, researchers and government participants and documented regional questions, constraints and priorities for future blue-carbon research and demonstration projects. It primarily transferred knowledge and strengthened networks; it did not generate a new regional carbon-stock inventory, approve a restoration project, establish a crediting methodology or issue carbon credits. Recommendations and finance opportunities identified through the project remained non-binding and required subsequent project development and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed science-transfer project, implemented from June 2016 to October 2018.

document_title: Land Use and Environmental Effects on Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Carbon Sequestration in Pacific Northwest Tidal Wetlands
notes: This collaborative research project quantified how greenhouse-gas emissions, carbon accumulation and net climate benefits vary among Pacific Northwest tidal-wetland types and land uses. Field work across multiple estuaries examined marshes, swamps, restored wetlands and altered lands, while the project expanded the regional blue-carbon database and contributed data for validation of a national methane-emissions model. Results supported development of regional calculators, mapping tools and climate-mitigation policy applications. The project strengthened accounting evidence by showing that methane emissions and carbon accumulation depend on salinity, hydrology, restoration history and local site conditions. It did not create a regulatory inventory requirement, certify credits or authorize restoration. Use of the results in carbon accounting or markets still requires project-specific baselines, uncertainty treatment and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from October 2020 to September 2024.

document_title: Do Prescribed Burns of Phragmites Australis Increase Denitrification and Carbon Sequestration?
notes: This collaborative research project evaluated the biogeochemical and ecosystem-service effects of using prescribed fire to manage invasive Phragmites in Delaware tidal marshes. Researchers compared marshes with different burn histories and examined soil and sediment characteristics, denitrification, vegetation response, carbon storage and the possible role of fire-derived biochar. The programme also synthesized evidence and engaged management agencies through a regional advisory process so that burn decisions could account for carbon and other ecosystem services. The work assessed an existing management practice rather than establishing a new carbon-removal project. It did not authorize prescribed burning, quantify creditable removals under an approved methodology or issue offsets. Findings remain conditional on site conditions, burn frequency, hydrology and the distinction between carbon stocks, emissions and net long-term sequestration.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project; the official project materials describe work beginning in October 2021 and concluding after the funded study period.

document_title: Testing Low-cost, Ultra-portable, Carbon Dioxide Sensors for Monitoring Salt Marsh Ecosystem Services, Resilience, and Restoration
notes: This multi-reserve catalyst project tested low-cost, portable sensor packages for measuring carbon-dioxide fluxes, temperature and humidity in salt-marsh environments. The project responded to the high cost and labor requirements of conventional greenhouse-gas monitoring and worked with reserve staff to improve instrument usability under routine field conditions. It produced shared field experience, datasets and a monitoring protocol intended to expand in-situ carbon-flux measurement capacity across the National Estuarine Research Reserve System. The programme supported MRV-related research and restoration evaluation but did not create a legally required monitoring standard, certify the sensor system for carbon-credit verification or establish that its measurements alone are sufficient for offset issuance. Longer time series, calibration, quality assurance and project-specific accounting remain necessary.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed catalyst project, implemented from October 2023 to September 2024.

document_title: Evaluating the Impact of Hydrologic Alterations on Salt Marsh Sustainability in a Changing Climate
notes: This collaborative research programme examined how historic ditching, drainage, tidal hydrology and sea-level rise affect salt-marsh elevation, carbon burial and other ecosystem services. Scientists and end users co-developed the Marsh2D decision-support framework to compare hydrologic management options and their trade-offs under future conditions. The project generated field data, model code, visual tools and management guidance for agencies and practitioners considering ditch maintenance, remediation or other interventions. Its principal contribution was evidence and decision support rather than direct implementation. The programme did not authorize hydrologic modification, prescribe a single restoration design, establish a carbon-credit methodology or quantify guaranteed removals. Application of its outputs remains site-specific and must account for ecological risk, permitting requirements and uncertainty in long-term marsh response.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project; official materials place the funded work between November 2017 and the end of the project period.

document_title: A Long-Term Perspective on Tidal Wetland Restoration: Vegetation Development, Elevation Capital, and Carbon Sequestration in the Oldest Projects Along the U.S. West Coast
notes: This multi-site project assessed some of the oldest tidal-marsh restoration sites on the United States West Coast and compared them with reference marshes. The work examined vegetation development, elevation capital, carbon storage and long-term recovery across sites in California, Oregon and Washington. Outputs included regional datasets, scientific publications and management guidance intended to improve future restoration design and monitoring. By studying projects several decades after intervention, the programme addressed evidence gaps that cannot be resolved through short project cycles. It was a completed research assessment and did not itself implement new restoration, approve project permits, establish a carbon-credit baseline or issue credits. Transfer of the findings to other wetland types or regions requires consideration of local sediment supply, hydrology, vegetation and sea-level conditions.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from October 2022 to September 2024.

document_title: Assessing Blue Carbon Storage at Restoration Sites of Various Ages and Morphologies
notes: This ongoing NOAA project quantifies carbon stocks, greenhouse-gas fluxes, sediment carbon and biomass at coastal sites restored through different techniques and at different times. Study designs include thin-layer placement of dredged sediment, living shorelines and beneficial use of dredged material to construct estuarine islands. The objective is to determine how quickly restored habitats develop carbon-storage functions comparable with natural systems and how restoration design affects possible eligibility for carbon offsets. The work directly supports blue-carbon accounting and restoration evaluation but remains a research programme. It does not certify any site, establish ownership of carbon benefits, approve offset issuance or replace the additionality, permanence, leakage and verification requirements of an applicable carbon standard.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Ongoing NCCOS research project that began in September 2022.

document_title: Ecological Impacts of Sea Level Rise on Flood Protection and Blue Carbon Capture in Pacific Northwest Wetlands
notes: This NCCOS research project evaluated how restored and natural tidal marshes and forested coastal wetlands in Coos Bay, Oregon, and Grays Bay, Washington, may provide flood buffering and blue-carbon benefits under sea-level-rise scenarios. The project combined hydrodynamic modeling, wetland-elevation modeling, existing datasets and new field observations of greenhouse-gas emissions and carbon sequestration. Its outputs were intended to help managers compare restoration and future climate scenarios and sustain multiple wetland services. The project supplied risk and planning evidence rather than a deployment decision. It did not require restoration, set a regulatory carbon-accounting method, validate a carbon project or issue offsets. Projected benefits depend on local hydrology, elevation change, salinity, vegetation and future sea-level conditions.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Completed NCCOS research project, conducted from September 2019 through the projected completion period in August 2022.

subnational_area: Maryland — Deal Island Wildlife Management Area
document_title: Evaluating the Beneficial Use of Sediment in a Microtidal Salt Marsh
notes: This ongoing NOAA assessment evaluates a marsh-elevation enhancement project at Deal Island, Maryland, where dredged sediment was placed on a deteriorating salt marsh and native vegetation was subsequently planted. Researchers established pre-placement baselines for vegetation, elevation, sedimentation and carbon stocks and are continuing post-placement monitoring to determine ecological effects, resilience and changes in carbon burial. The programme links a real restoration intervention with long-term performance assessment and therefore provides evidence relevant to natural infrastructure and blue-carbon accounting. It does not itself constitute the underlying project permit, establish an offset methodology or confirm that increased carbon storage is additional, permanent and creditable. Results remain dependent on continued monitoring and comparison with pre-restoration conditions.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Ongoing NCCOS monitoring and assessment project; baseline work began in 2021 and sediment placement was completed in 2024.

document_title: Managing Mangroves and Production Landscapes for Climate Change Mitigation
notes: GEF Project 9521 supports protection and restoration of approximately 1,500 hectares of mangroves and rehabilitation of about 1,200 hectares of degraded rice fields in Guinea-Bissau. The project links climate mitigation with food security and production-landscape management and is implemented through an international environmental-finance framework with national executing partners. The official project page records a GEF grant, substantial co-financing and formal project approval. The programme constitutes direct restoration and enabling finance, but the available project summary does not establish a carbon-credit registry, guarantee quantified removals or indicate that credits have been issued. Carbon outcomes depend on successful ecological restoration, avoided degradation, monitoring and treatment of land-use and community safeguards throughout implementation.
source: Global Environment Facility (GEF)
status_note: GEF full-size project approved for implementation in August 2018; the official GEF page lists the project as approved.

document_title: Blue Economy for Resilient Africa Program — Mangrove Blue Carbon Pilot Program
notes: The World Bank announced a USD 13.5 million Mangrove Blue Carbon Pilot Program in Ghana under the Blue Economy for Resilient Africa Program and the West Africa Coastal Areas Management Program. The financing package combined IDA and PROBLUE resources with private funding and was intended to support planting, technical assistance and maintenance of approximately 3,000 hectares of mangroves over a twenty-year period. The programme is an implementation and blended-finance initiative rather than a general policy statement. The announcement does not by itself establish a national carbon-credit methodology, confirm project registration or report issued credits. Long-term climate benefits depend on restoration survival, maintenance, community participation, land and carbon rights, environmental safeguards and credible monitoring of additional and durable carbon gains.
source: World Bank
status_note: Announced in November 2022 as a financed long-term mangrove pilot under the World Bank's African blue-economy programme.

document_title: Costa Rica Marine Payment for Environmental Services Pilot for Mangrove Conservation
notes: Costa Rica launched its first marine Payment for Environmental Services pilot for mangrove conservation in the Gulf of Nicoya with World Bank support and Earthshot Prize funding. The arrangement involves national environmental, conservation, fisheries and finance institutions and community associations representing mollusk gatherers. Participants receive recurring payments tied to verified compliance with conservation, monitoring, surveillance, restocking and sustainable-use activities under approved management plans. The pilot extends results-based environmental finance from terrestrial forests to marine-coastal ecosystems and covers more than 6,000 hectares of mangroves. It is an ecological-compensation mechanism, not automatically a tradable carbon-credit programme. The official description does not state that offsets are issued, transferred or usable for compliance, and payments reward verified stewardship rather than a quantified volume of additional carbon removal.
source: Government of Costa Rica / World Bank
status_note: Active pilot formalized through an inter-institutional cooperation arrangement and supported by a national executive decree.

document_title: Thailand Blue Economy Financing and Blue Carbon Credit Readiness Assistance
notes: The World Bank technical-assistance package supports Thailand's development of blue-economy finance, coastal protection and sustainable ocean planning. It includes work toward a sovereign blue bond, integrated seascape management and financing structures under which mangrove restoration may be organized to generate blue-carbon credits and attract private capital. The initiative is relevant to policy readiness, finance design and possible market integration rather than evidence that a functioning blue-carbon credit programme already exists. The official announcement does not identify an approved mangrove methodology, registered project, issued credit volume or compliance-market recognition. Any future credits would still require clear project boundaries, additionality, carbon rights, safeguards, monitoring, verification and consistency with Thailand's broader carbon-market and sustainable-finance rules.
source: World Bank / Government of Thailand
status_note: Active World Bank technical-assistance and financing-readiness initiative announced in September 2025.

document_title: Yale Blue Carbon Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement Initiative
notes: The Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture launched a Blue Carbon Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement initiative to investigate whether alkalinity generated through mangrove and other blue-carbon ecosystem processes can provide a durable, measurable carbon-removal benefit and a new source of restoration finance. The programme combines field monitoring at restoration sites, mechanistic research, method development, stakeholder workshops and engagement with carbon registries. Planned outputs include best-practice guidance, MRV approaches and protocol-development field trials. The initiative is explicitly at the research and methodology-development stage. It has not established an approved crediting protocol, demonstrated that all measured alkalinity represents additional atmospheric carbon removal, authorized deliberate alkalinity deployment or reported issued credits. Ecological safeguards, attribution, transport, durability and double-counting remain central research questions.
source: Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture (YCNCC)
status_note: Active research initiative launched in 2025, with MRV and protocol-development work continuing in 2026.

document_title: Salt Marsh Ecology in an Era of Sea Level Rise
notes: This long-term NOAA research project examined whether North Carolina salt marshes can maintain elevation and carbon-storage functions as sea level rises. Field surveys, experimental studies, surface-elevation tables and simulation models were used to connect tidal inundation, sediment accretion, above- and below-ground plant growth, root decay and the persistence of carbon in marsh soils. The project generated evidence on the conditions under which marshes may continue to accumulate blue carbon while remaining physically sustainable. It was an ecological research and monitoring programme rather than a restoration authorization or carbon-market instrument. The work did not establish a mandatory accounting method, validate a project baseline, determine additionality or permanence for crediting purposes, or issue carbon credits.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Completed NOAA research project conducted from January 2004 through December 2018.

document_title: Establishing a Blue Carbon Network for the Gulf Coast
notes: This NOAA-funded science-transfer project established a Gulf Coast blue-carbon network for reserve staff, local governments, researchers, restoration practitioners, nonprofit organizations and resource managers. The network was designed to share scientific information, coordinate regional activities, support locally relevant tools and projects, and test ways of using the recognized value of coastal carbon to attract funding for wetland conservation and restoration. The project therefore addressed capacity, coordination and early-stage finance readiness rather than directly restoring a specified site. It did not create a regional carbon registry, approve a crediting methodology, establish ownership of carbon benefits, register an offset project or issue credits. Any subsequent restoration or market activity required independent project design, permitting, accounting, safeguards and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed science-transfer project implemented from September 2015 through August 2017.

document_title: Is macroalgal carbon sequestration the 'elephant in the Blue Carbon room'?
notes: This NERC studentship investigates the contribution of exported macroalgal carbon to long-term burial and benthic food webs in the deep Arctic fjord of Kongsfjorden. The project uses an existing digital landscape model, sediment-carbon information and field observations to build a geographically constrained inventory of macroalgae-derived blue carbon and to distinguish sequestration from biological consumption and remineralization. Its purpose is to reduce major uncertainty surrounding the fate of carbon exported from macroalgal source habitats and to support translation of evidence into United Kingdom blue-carbon policy discussions. The project studies natural carbon pathways and does not authorize macroalgae cultivation, deliberate biomass sinking or commercial deployment. It has not established a crediting protocol, verified removals or issued carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a funded study period from September 2020 through August 2027.

document_title: The Significance of Macroalgal Detritus for Marine Food Webs and Blue-Carbon Sequestration
notes: This NERC studentship quantified how macroalgal detritus contributes to carbon burial and marine food webs in Scottish fjords. The project combined seabed-camera surveys, sediment coring, stable-isotope analysis, isotope-tracing experiments, food-web modeling and geographic information systems to develop a first-order assessment of the carbon subsidy transferred from macroalgal habitats into deeper sea-loch sediments. It addressed uncertainty over whether exported macroalgal material is durably sequestered, consumed or remineralized and was connected to the Scottish Blue Carbon Forum to support policy relevance. The research did not constitute a macroalgae farming or biomass-sinking project, did not authorize intervention in marine ecosystems, and did not establish project-level additionality, permanence, ownership or an approved carbon-credit methodology.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC studentship with a study period from September 2020 through January 2026.

document_title: Migration of CO2 through North Sea Geological Carbon Storage Sites: Impact of Faults, Geological Heterogeneities and Dissolution
notes: This NERC research grant examined the security of offshore geological carbon storage by quantifying CO2 migration, dissolution and capillary trapping in faults and heterogeneous strata representative of North Sea reservoir overburden. Work associated with the Goldeneye field combined geological characterization, core experiments, geochemical analysis, analogue flow experiments and seismic assessment to improve predictions of leakage pathways and the detectability of CO2 above a storage reservoir. The project generated scientific tools relevant to operators and regulators evaluating offshore storage integrity. It was a risk-reduction research programme, not a storage permit or injection authorization. It did not approve the Goldeneye site, establish a legally binding monitoring plan, certify stored volumes or demonstrate that any carbon credits or compliance units had been issued.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant implemented from April 2016 through April 2021.

subnational_area: North Sea and Ardmucknish Bay, Scotland
document_title: Quantifying and Monitoring Potential Ecosystem Impacts of Geological Carbon Storage
notes: The QICS research project conducted a controlled, small-scale sub-seabed CO2 release experiment to quantify how leakage from geological storage could affect marine sediments, water chemistry, microorganisms and benthic communities. The programme measured the movement and fate of released CO2, evaluated ecosystem response and recovery, tested geophysical and biogeochemical monitoring techniques, and developed models and recommendations for early leakage detection and environmental risk assessment. Its results became an evidence base for planning and monitoring offshore carbon-storage demonstrations. The experiment was scientific research under controlled conditions and did not authorize commercial storage or routine marine release. The project did not issue a storage permit, establish a binding regulatory standard, certify stored quantities or create carbon credits, although its monitoring findings may inform later regulatory and verification systems.
source: British Geological Survey / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant conducted from April 2010 through April 2015.

document_title: Characterization of Major Overburden Leakage Pathways above Sub-seafloor CO2 Storage Reservoirs in the North Sea (CHIMNEY)
notes: The CHIMNEY project investigated near-vertical geological structures that could provide leakage pathways above sub-seafloor CO2 storage reservoirs in the North Sea. Researchers combined marine seismic imaging, ocean-bottom instruments, drilling and core analysis, rock-physics experiments, fluid chemistry and three-dimensional modeling to estimate pathway continuity, permeability and potential leakage scenarios. Outputs were intended to improve overburden characterization, storage-site monitoring and regulatory confidence under offshore carbon-storage rules and international marine agreements. This record represents the transferred continuation award shown by UKRI rather than a separate commercial storage operation. The project did not authorize CO2 injection, approve a storage complex, establish a binding site-monitoring plan, quantify creditable removals or issue carbon credits. Its contribution was scientific methodology and risk evidence.
source: National Oceanography Centre / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed transferred NERC research award implemented from November 2019 through October 2021; it continued an earlier grant that began in 2016.

document_title: Empowering Coastal Communities through Seagrass Restoration and Fisheries Sustainability Project
notes: This Gulf of Gabes initiative was selected as one of six flagship carbon projects supported by the IUCN-managed WALD Innovation Facility, which provides early-stage grants of up to EUR 1.5 million per project. The Tunisia project combines marine ecosystem restoration with sustainable fishing practices to improve climate resilience, ecosystem condition and coastal livelihoods. The wider facility is intended to move high-integrity nature-based projects toward investment readiness while applying biodiversity, community, transparency and benefit-sharing safeguards. The announcement confirms project selection but provides no detailed restoration area, implementation schedule, approved methodology, registry status or quantified removal volume for the Tunisia activity. It therefore represents funded project preparation and prospective restoration, not evidence that carbon credits have been registered, verified or issued.
source: International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) / WALD Innovation Facility
status_note: Selected for WALD Innovation Facility grant support in October 2025; detailed implementation and credit-registration status were not stated in the official announcement.

document_title: Estimating Global Carbon Storage of Mangrove Ecosystems
notes: This World Bank technical report developed global estimates of mangrove biomass and soil-organic-carbon stocks using harmonized spatial datasets. It reports carbon stocks and changes for 122 countries with mangrove extent and provides comparisons by region and income group for multiple observation years between 1996 and 2020. The work was designed to strengthen natural-capital evidence, national and regional planning, restoration prioritization and understanding of uncertainty in global mangrove carbon estimates. It is an analytical report rather than a regulatory inventory rule or project-level methodology. The estimates do not establish additionality, permanence, leakage, ownership or a verified baseline for individual carbon projects, and the report does not authorize restoration, certify national greenhouse-gas submissions, register offsets or issue carbon credits.
source: World Bank
status_note: Published World Bank technical report issued in 2024 and available as an active evidence resource.

document_title: Just How 'Green' Is the Grass on the Other Side? Particulate Carbon and Microplastic Capture Potential by Seagrass Meadows in Wales
notes: This active NERC studentship studies how the structure, condition and environmental setting of temperate seagrass meadows influence the capture of particulate carbon and microplastics in Wales. Broad-scale surveys and manipulative field and laboratory experiments examine factors such as meadow density, biomass, rhizome depth, epiphyte load, sediment grain size, nutrient input, physical disturbance and surrounding macroalgae. The project is intended to improve management of seagrass ecosystem services and address uncertainty about the relationship between habitat condition and carbon capture. It is scientific research rather than a restoration programme or crediting system. The study does not establish that all captured particulate carbon is durably sequestered, approve a monitoring standard, authorize seagrass intervention or generate verified carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a study period from September 2024 through March 2028.

document_title: Effects of Ozone on Carbon Sequestration by Mangroves
notes: This active NERC studentship investigates whether ozone pollution reduces the carbon-sequestration capacity of mangrove ecosystems. The project combines international field studies, controlled ozone-exposure experiments and predictive modeling to assess present-day impacts, identify ecological characteristics associated with ozone sensitivity, and map where vulnerable mangroves overlap with global ozone-pollution hotspots. Its expected contribution is an improved evidence base for mangrove conservation and climate policy, particularly where atmospheric pollution may weaken anticipated carbon benefits. The work does not directly restore or expand mangroves, establish a carbon-credit project, define a national inventory method or authorize deployment. It also does not assume that standing carbon stocks equal additional removals; the magnitude, persistence and policy implications of ozone-related effects remain research questions.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a study period from September 2024 through March 2028.

document_title: Recovery of Seagrass for Ocean Wealth UK (ReSOW UK)
notes: ReSOW UK was a national research programme designed to build the scientific, spatial, economic and governance evidence needed for large-scale seagrass recovery. The consortium combined field measurements, Earth observation, habitat-suitability analysis, social science, natural-capital accounting and stakeholder engagement to map existing and potential seagrass, quantify carbon and fisheries benefits, identify barriers to restoration, and develop a Coastal Ecosystem Enhancement Decision Support Tool. The programme supported restoration planning and financing discussions with public agencies and practitioners, but the grant itself did not authorize restoration at specific sites or establish a national seagrass carbon-credit methodology. It did not register projects or issue credits, and any future intervention still requires site-specific ecological assessment, permissions, additionality analysis, safeguards and long-term monitoring.
source: National Oceanography Centre / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)
status_note: Completed research grant implemented from November 2021 through December 2025.

document_title: Carbon Storage in Intertidal Environments (C-SIDE)
notes: C-SIDE produced a national-scale assessment of carbon storage and burial in British salt marshes. Research across contrasting coastal regions combined sediment cores, radioisotope dating, vegetation and soil measurements, source attribution, citizen science, historical mapping, three-dimensional habitat mapping and statistical modeling to identify controls on carbon stocks and accumulation rates. The project generated extensive datasets and evidence intended to support coastal management, natural-capital assessment, greenhouse-gas inventory development and evaluation of managed realignment or salt-marsh creation. It was a completed research programme rather than a restoration authorization or formal accounting standard. The outputs do not independently establish project additionality, permanence, leakage or ownership, and the grant did not register carbon projects, certify national inventory values or issue credits.
source: University of St Andrews / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant implemented from May 2018 through May 2023.

document_title: Scalable, Multiparameter Chip-Size Carbon Sensors
notes: This ARPA-E SEA-CO2 project funds Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to develop a system-on-a-chip for ocean carbon-flux monitoring. The proposed miniature device integrates measurements such as pH, oxygen and particulate organic carbon while reducing power demand, instrument size and manufacturing cost for use on gliders and profiling floats. Semiconductor fabrication and scalable calibration are intended to replace hand-built, small-batch sensor production and support broader marine carbon dioxide removal monitoring. The award is a research and technology-development activity, not an approved MRV standard, commercial verification service or field-deployment authorization. The official description does not state that the sensor has completed operational validation, certified removals or supported issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official project description presents an active research and sensor-development award without reporting commercial deployment or credit issuance.

document_title: Acoustic Methods for mCDR Based on Blue Carbon Burial in Seagrass Meadows
notes: The University of Texas at Austin SEA-CO2 project develops an acoustic sensor network to estimate biological activity and carbon burial in shallow seagrass meadows. The system is designed to detect oxygen bubbles released during photosynthesis and use sound refraction through the seabed to estimate carbon stored in roots and sediments. ARPA-E presents the technology as a lower-cost monitoring approach for large-scale seagrass remediation and marine carbon dioxide removal assessment. The award supports measurement development and validation rather than the restoration of a specified meadow. It does not establish an approved blue-carbon methodology, determine project additionality or permanence, authorize habitat intervention, register a carbon project or confirm that credits have been issued.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active acoustic MRV research project; no restoration permit, registry approval or issued credits are reported.

document_title: SLEUTH: Spectroscopy of Oceanic Liquid Environments Using Towed Optical Sensor Heads
notes: The University of Colorado Boulder SEA-CO2 project develops an optical underwater sensing system for dissolved carbon compounds. A sensor head using dual-frequency-comb laser-stimulated Raman spectroscopy is intended to be towed beneath an autonomous wave-energy-harvesting surface vehicle through an optical-fiber cable. The objective is to transfer laboratory spectroscopy into persistent, mobile and in-situ ocean observations that can improve spatial coverage for marine carbon dioxide removal measurement. The project is an early-stage instrumentation award rather than an operational monitoring network. The official description does not report completed marine deployment, a legally required MRV protocol, quantified atmospheric carbon removal, third-party verification or carbon-credit issuance, and it does not authorize any particular mCDR intervention.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official material describes ongoing instrument development and does not report operational certification or verified removals.

document_title: SEAfloor Self-Sustaining CO2 Assessment Probe Edge (SEASCAPE)
notes: The University of Utah SEA-CO2 project develops low-power micro-optical and micro-electronic probes for long-duration measurement of carbon accumulation in marine sediments. Groups of probes are intended to be inserted across broad seafloor areas and operate for more than one year while measuring carbon dioxide and pH through a novel bubble-based mechanism. The project aims to address calibration, energy-consumption and sensor-degradation constraints that limit persistent seafloor carbon monitoring. It is an instrumentation-development award and not a marine geological storage permit or approved verification protocol. The official description does not demonstrate operational deployment at a commercial storage site, establish project additionality or permanence, certify stored carbon or report issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active seafloor-sensor development project; commercial validation and regulatory acceptance are not reported.

document_title: Spatially Resolved Multi-Parameter Sensing of Ocean Carbon Dynamics Using Fiber-Optic Time-of-Flight Sensors
notes: GE Research's SEA-CO2 award develops a fiber-optic sensor cable intended to measure multiple chemical ocean-carbon parameters across kilometer-scale transects while being towed from marine vessels. Chemically responsive polymer coatings distribute sensing capability along a continuous optical fiber, potentially expanding the volume observed and reducing costs relative to stationary or slowly lowered point sensors. The project supports spatially resolved marine carbon dioxide removal monitoring and the development of scalable observation technology. It remains an R&D project rather than an operational MRV service or mandatory standard. The official description does not report completed field qualification, accepted uncertainty thresholds, quantified removals, regulatory approval or issuance of carbon credits based on the sensing system.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the project remains technology development and the official description does not report completed certification or credit use.

document_title: Computational Systems for Tracking Ocean Carbon (C-Star)
notes: The C-Star SEA-CO2 project led by [C]Worthy develops a community framework for marine carbon accounting, model construction and data assimilation. The proposed system combines observational and forcing datasets, an ocean general-circulation model, biogeochemistry, tracers, marine carbon dioxide removal modules and ecosystem components to estimate ocean state and treatment effects. Its purpose is to improve transparency, reproducibility and accuracy in model-based MRV across mCDR approaches. The award builds research infrastructure and does not itself establish a legally binding accounting methodology or carbon-credit registry. The official description does not specify that the framework has completed independent validation, achieved an accepted error threshold, verified a commercial removal project or supported issuance of tradable credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active modeling and data-assimilation project; formal methodology approval and credit use are not reported.

document_title: Hybrid Distributed pH, CO2, Temperature and Acoustic Sensing for Monitoring and Verification of Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: The University of Pittsburgh SEA-CO2 project develops buoy-mounted optical-fiber sensors for continuous measurement of pH, carbon dioxide, temperature and acoustic conditions from the ocean surface to the seafloor. Chemically selective coatings are integrated into low-cost commercial fibers using a reel-to-reel manufacturing approach intended to support large-scale production. The technology is designed for nearshore mCDR applications including ecosystem recovery, ocean alkalinity enhancement and electrochemical processes that require persistent monitoring. This is a funded sensor-development project, not an approved environmental monitoring requirement or operational verification service. The official description does not report completed field validation, a standardized uncertainty framework, authorization of an mCDR intervention, certified removal quantities or carbon-credit issuance.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official project description reports technology development but no completed regulatory qualification or verified removals.

document_title: Integrated Experimental and Modeling Assessment of Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement for Scalable Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's SEA-CO2 project combines numerical modeling with mesocosm experiments to evaluate ocean alkalinity enhancement effectiveness and ecological impacts in three major United States coastal settings. Tank experiments provide ground-truth data for models intended to estimate how treatment size, location, frequency and duration influence carbon removal and ocean-acidification mitigation. The award supports technology assessment, model validation and environmental evidence needed before responsible scale-up. It does not authorize alkalinity addition in open waters, define a binding national OAE methodology or establish a carbon-credit programme. The official project description does not report a completed field deployment, independently verified net removal, accepted durability calculation or issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active model and mesocosm assessment; no open-water deployment authorization or issued credits are reported.

document_title: Development of Thin-Film Composite Hollow-Fiber Membranes for Direct Ocean Capture
notes: ARPA-E funded Captura to develop low-cost thin-film composite hollow-fiber membranes for stripping carbon dioxide from ocean water. The project modifies inexpensive water-filtration fibers with highly CO2-permeable coatings and uses computationally assisted contactor design to improve counterflow and cross-flow gas transfer. Its stated objective is to reduce the capital cost of the CO2 stripping stage and validate a direct ocean capture component at laboratory scale. The project page identifies a September 2022 start and March 2026 end date and lists the award as Alumni. It was a technology-development project rather than a commercial deployment permit, ocean discharge authorization or carbon-credit methodology, and the official page does not report issued credits or independently verified net removals.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: ARPA-E lists the project as Alumni, with a funded period from 6 September 2022 through 5 March 2026.

document_title: Electrochemically Modulated CO2 Removal from Ocean Waters
notes: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology ARPA-E project develops a battery-like electro-swing process that releases dissolved CO2 from seawater through electrochemical proton-gradient control and then alkalizes the treated water before its return. The approach is designed to avoid chemical additives and costly membranes while allowing compact systems to operate on platforms or ships using renewable electricity. ARPA-E lists the project as Active with a funded period from February 2021 through September 2026. The award supports engineering research and prototype development, not commercial offshore operation or a discharge permit. The official page does not report full-system field validation, independently verified atmospheric removal, storage certification, an approved crediting methodology or issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: ARPA-E lists the project as Active, with a funded period from 24 February 2021 through 30 September 2026.

document_title: Hydrolytic Softening of Ocean Water for Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: The University of North Dakota Energy and Environmental Research Center received ARPA-E support to develop hydrolytic softening for direct ocean carbon dioxide removal. The process adapts conventional water-softening chemistry by precipitating dissolved inorganic carbon as calcium carbonate, decomposing the precipitate to release a concentrated CO2 stream, and regenerating lime for repeated use. ARPA-E describes a potential energy-cost reduction relative to sodium-chloride splitting with bipolar membrane electrodialysis. The project ran from May 2021 to November 2022 and is listed as Alumni. It was a completed early-stage research award and did not authorize offshore operation, establish a storage pathway, verify lifecycle net removal, create a carbon-credit methodology or issue credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
